messages.content:
Compute the largest positive integer \( n \) such that

\[
n \text{ divides } (\lfloor \sqrt{n} \rfloor)!^{n!} + 450.
\]

Put your final answer within \boxed{}.

message.content:
Let

\[
m=\lfloor \sqrt{n}\rfloor.
\]

We analyze the prime-power divisors of \(n\). Suppose \(p^a\parallel n\), where \(p\) is prime and \(a=v_p(n)\).

### 1. Prime factors with \(p\le m\)

Since \(p\le m\), we have \(p\mid m!\). Therefore

\[
p^{n!}\mid (m!)^{n!}.
\]

Also \(p^a\le n\), so \(a\le n\le n!\). Hence

\[
p^a\mid (m!)^{n!}.
\]

Thus, modulo \(p^a\),

\[
(m!)^{n!}+450 \equiv 450 \pmod{p^a}.
\]

Since \(n\) divides the whole expression and \(p^a\mid n\), we must have

\[
p^a\mid 450.
\]

So every prime power of \(n\) whose prime is \(\le m\) must divide \(450\).

### 2. Prime factors with \(p>m\)

If \(p>m\), then \(p>\sqrt n\), so \(p^2>n\). Thus \(p\) appears to the first power in \(n\).

Also \(p\le n\), so \(p-1\le n\), meaning \(p-1\mid n!\). Since \(p>m\), \(p\nmid m!\). By Fermat’s little theorem,

\[
(m!)^{p-1}\equiv 1 \pmod p,
\]

so

\[
(m!)^{n!}\equiv 1 \pmod p.
\]

Therefore \(p\) divides the expression exactly when

\[
p\mid 1+450=451.
\]

Since

\[
451=11\cdot 41,
\]

any prime factor \(p>m\) must be either \(11\) or \(41\).

Moreover, at most one prime factor of \(n\) can be \(>\sqrt n\). If such a prime exists, say \(p\), write

\[
n=pd.
\]

Because \(p>\sqrt n\),

\[
d=\frac{n}{p}<\sqrt n,
\]

so every prime divisor of \(d\) is \(\le m\). By part 1, all prime powers of \(d\) divide \(450\), so

\[
d\mid 450.
\]

Also \(p^2>n=pd\), so \(d<p\).

### 3. Maximizing \(n\)

We now consider the possible cases:

- If no prime factor of \(n\) is \(>m\), then every prime power of \(n\) divides \(450\), so

\[
n\mid 450 \quad\Rightarrow\quad n\le 450.
\]

- If the large prime is \(p=11\), then \(d\mid 450\) and \(d<11\). The largest divisor of \(450\) less than \(11\) is \(10\), giving

\[
n\le 11\cdot 10=110.
\]

- If the large prime is \(p=41\), then \(d\mid 450\) and \(d<41\). The largest divisor of \(450\) less than \(41\) is \(30\), giving

\[
n\le 41\cdot 30=1230.
\]

Thus \(n\le 1230\).

### 4. Verification for \(n=1230\)

We have

\[
\sqrt{1230}\approx 35.07,
\]

so

\[
m=\lfloor\sqrt{1230}\rfloor=35.
\]

Also

\[
1230=2\cdot 3\cdot 5\cdot 41.
\]

For \(p=2,3,5\), each is \(\le 35\). Since each divides \(35!\), the term \((35!)^{1230!}\) is divisible by \(p\), and \(450\) is divisible by \(p\). Hence each of \(2,3,5\) divides the expression.

For \(p=41\), note that \(41>35\), so \(41\nmid 35!\). Since \(40\mid 1230!\), Fermat gives

\[
(35!)^{1230!}\equiv 1 \pmod{41}.
\]

Also

\[
450\equiv 40 \pmod{41},
\]

so

\[
(35!)^{1230!}+450\equiv 1+40\equiv 0 \pmod{41}.
\]

Thus \(41\) divides the expression. Since \(2,3,5,41\) are pairwise coprime, \(1230\) divides the expression.

Therefore the largest possible \(n\) is

\[
\boxed{1230}
\]
